title: Solomon's Building, Worship, and Trade
summary: After twenty years of building the temple and his palace, Solomon fortifies cities across his realm, campaigns at Hamath-zobah, and conscripts the remaining Canaanite peoples as laborers while Israelites serve as soldiers and officers. He moves Pharaoh's daughter out of the City of David because of the holiness of the ark, establishes the full order of sacrifices and festivals as Moses and David commanded, and sends ships with Hiram's sailors from Ezion-geber to Ophir for gold.
story: The temple has been dedicated and God has answered (chapters 5 to 7). This chapter surveys what Solomon did with the rest of his reign, and its center of gravity is still worship. Between notices about building, labor, and trade stands the heart of the chapter: Solomon's faithful ordering of sacrifices, feasts, priests, Levites, and gatekeepers exactly as Moses and David had commanded (verses 12-16). The summary line, “So the house of the LORD was completed” (verse 16), closes the building story that began in 1 Chronicles 22. Chapter 9 will show Solomon's fame reaching the nations.
historical:
The chapter parallels 1 Kings 9:10-28 but with differences. The twenty years of verse 1 combine the seven years spent on the temple and thirteen on the palace (1 Kings 6:38; 7:1), bringing us to about 950 BC. First Kings 9:15 also lists Hazor, Megiddo, and Gezer among Solomon's building projects. At those sites archaeologists found similar monumental gateways that the Israeli archaeologist Yigael Yadin attributed to Solomon; other scholars date them later, to the ninth century BC, and the dating remains debated.

Tadmor (verse 4) is the name of the later caravan city known in Greek and Roman times as Palmyra, in the Syrian desert. The parallel in 1 Kings 9:18 reads Tamar in the written Hebrew text, a place in the south of Judah, with Tadmor supplied as the traditional reading, so some scholars think Chronicles has updated the name. Hamath-zobah (verse 3), in Syria, is the only military campaign attributed to Solomon in Chronicles. Ezion-geber and Eloth (Elath) lay at the northern tip of the Gulf of Aqaba, Israel's outlet to the Red Sea and the trade routes to Arabia and East Africa. Beth-horon guarded the main road climbing from the coastal plain to Jerusalem.
cultural:
Store cities held grain, oil, and supplies for the army and administration, and chariot cities housed the royal chariot force. Such building programs were the ordinary work of ancient kings, and inscriptions from across the Near East boast of them. Conscripted labor (corvée) drawn from subject peoples was also standard. The note that Solomon did not make Israelites into slave laborers (verse 9) reflects the principle that Israelites, once freed from Egypt, were not to be made slaves of fellow Israelites.

The move of Pharaoh's daughter (verse 11) reflects Israel's concern with holiness. Solomon's marriage to an Egyptian princess was a diplomatic alliance, the kind of marriage ancient kings made to seal treaties. Chronicles explains why she was moved: the places the ark had entered were holy, and a foreign wife, presumably a worshiper of other gods, should not live there. The three annual feasts of verse 13 (Unleavened Bread with Passover in spring, Weeks at the wheat harvest, and Tabernacles in autumn) were the pilgrimage festivals when Israelite men were commanded to appear before the LORD (Deuteronomy 16:16).
literary: The chapter is a mosaic of short reports, but its arrangement is deliberate. Building and labor (verses 1-10) and trade (17-18) frame the central section on worship (11-16). The worship section piles up the language of faithful obedience: “according to the commandment of Moses”, “in keeping with the ordinances of his father David”, “the command of David, the man of God”, and “did not turn aside”. The Chronicler wants readers to see Solomon's reign at its height as a reign ordered around God's house and God's word. It is notable that David is called “the man of God” (verse 14), a title usually reserved for prophets, because he gave Israel its pattern of worship.

outline.t: Pharaoh's daughter moved from the City of David

doctrines.note: Solomon recognizes that the places the ark has entered are holy (verse 11). Holiness in the Old Testament is not only a moral quality but a claim on space: what belongs to God is set apart.

The daily, weekly, monthly, and annual offerings follow “the commandment of Moses” (verse 13). Israel's worship was not invented by its kings but received through Moses and ordered by David. Faithfulness means doing what God commanded.

The chapter shows the kingdom at peace and prosperity, with its king devoted to God's house. For the Chronicler's readers this was a picture of what the kingdom of God among his people looked like at its best.

words.note: Mitsvah, commandment. It appears three times in verses 13-15, tying Solomon's worship to the commands of Moses and David. A commandment is an authoritative word to be obeyed, and the chapter's worship section is built around keeping it.

Chag, feast or pilgrimage festival. The word is related to the Arabic hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca, and names the three great annual feasts when Israel traveled to the sanctuary. Israel's calendar was structured around these celebrations of God's acts in the exodus and the harvest.

Sho'er, gatekeeper. Gatekeepers guarded the temple gates, controlled access, and cared for the storerooms and treasuries (1 Chronicles 26). The Chronicler's interest in them reflects his interest in the Levites, among whom they were counted, and perhaps his own world.

Ophir, the source of Solomon's gold. Its location is unknown; suggestions include southwestern Arabia, the Horn of Africa, and India. An inscribed potsherd from Tell Qasile near Tel Aviv, dated to around the eighth century BC, mentions gold of Ophir, confirming that the name was used for a real source of gold.

christ: The chapter shows a son of David who gives his reign to ordering the worship of God: daily sacrifices, Sabbaths, new moons, and feasts, all according to God's command. The New Testament presents Jesus as the son of David who both keeps the law perfectly and fulfills what the sacrifices and festivals pointed to. Paul calls Christ our Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7), the fulfillment of the Feast of Unleavened Bread; the Spirit was given at the Feast of Weeks, Pentecost (Acts 2:1); and John sets Jesus' great invitation to the thirsty at the Feast of Tabernacles (John 7:2, 37-39). Colossians 2:16-17 calls festivals, new moons, and Sabbaths a shadow of things to come, whose substance belongs to Christ. The link here is typological: the festivals Solomon organized became, in the New Testament's reading, pointers to Christ.

hard.q: Did Hiram give cities to Solomon, or did Solomon give cities to Hiram?
hard.a: Verse 2 says Solomon rebuilt the cities Hiram had given him. First Kings 9:10-14 says the opposite: Solomon gave Hiram twenty towns in Galilee, which Hiram found unsatisfactory and called Cabul, apparently meaning something like worthless. Interpreters have proposed several solutions. One is that Hiram, displeased, returned the towns to Solomon, who then rebuilt and settled them, so both accounts describe stages of the same transaction. Another is that the towns were collateral or payment exchanged in a larger deal (Kings mentions 120 talents of gold sent by Hiram), and that each account highlights a different side of it. Some scholars think the Chronicler deliberately presented the transaction in a way more flattering to Solomon, since his portrait of Solomon omits most of his failings. The texts don't let us decide with certainty, but the harmonizing suggestion that Hiram returned the towns is plausible and widely held.

questions: The chapter places the ordering of worship at the center of a busy reign of building and trade. What is at the center of your busy life?
Solomon moved his wife out of the City of David because of the holiness of the ark, yet kept the marriage. What does this suggest about the tension between holiness and compromise?
Israel's year was shaped by feasts remembering what God had done. How does your calendar help you remember God's work?
